newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-ABARE sees bumper Australia summer harvest.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-ABARE sees bumper Australia summer harvest.

text.p: Australia's total summer crop production is expected to rise six percent in 1996/97 (July-June), to a record 3.85 million tonnes, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday.

The forecast for a bumper summer crop was due largely to expected record cotton and rice production, and an increase of more 50 percent in sunflower production, ABARE said in its Australian Crop Report.
The summer forecasts followed a winter harvest of unprecedented size, ABARE executive director Brian Fisher said in a statement.
They also came in spite of a slight decline in overall summer crop plantings, as well as too much high rainfall in some of the northwest of New South Wales and too little in parts of Queensland.
ABARE said the weather outlook for the three months to April 1997 indicated that normal rainfall patterns were the most likely possibility.
This would consolidate promising yield prospects for the remainder of the summer growing season, and provide at least average subsoil moisture levels for the planting of the 1997/98 winter crop.
Total summer plantings were estimated at just over 1.3 milion hectares in 1996/97, 1.7 percent lower than in 1995/96.
Production in Queensland state was expected to decline 27 percent due to a fall in the area sown, while production in New South Wales state was forecast to be up 30 percent.

ABARE said harvest conditions for the 1996/97 winter crop were generally favourable in all states except Western Australia, and yields were above average in New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and South Australia.
Total Australian winter crop production for 1996/97 was estimated to be a record 34.5 million tonnes, more than four million tonnes higher than the previous record set in 1983-84.
The 1996/97 wheat harvest was estimated at 23.5 million tonnes, 1.5 million tonnes higher than the previous 1983/84 record, and was above average in terms of quality, ABARE said.
Total plantings to winter crops in 1997/98 were forecast to decline about 2.5 percent on the previous year, reflecting an expectation of lower prices, ABARE said.
